description:
Most techy couple :) We are a team of two from Dushanbe, Tajikistan, and we like finding things that move.

For Planet X and SPHEREx we built Skyblink: a ten-second flipbook of two real NASA SPHEREx photos and one question, "Did something move?" Software searches first, people judge, and every claim is tested against a known answer: 172 of 182 known asteroids recovered.

Python pipeline, Rust server, Next.js site, open source. Play a round: dchr.koinotinav.com/skyblink
summary:
SPHEREx photographs the whole sky twice a year, and anything close to us gives itself away by moving between photographs. There is far too much sky for one person. Skyblink turns the SPHEREx archive into ten-second tasks: you watch two real photographs of the same patch of sky, taken hours apart, flip back and forth, and answer one question, "did something move?".

Software goes first. It compares pairs of SPHEREx frames matched in wavelength, measures about 50,000 sources per pair, and keeps the patches where a dot is in one photograph and missing from the other. People judge those patches. Known asteroids and test dots that we plant ourselves are mixed into the feed, so each volunteer's reliability is measured, and reliable answers weigh more. The result is a public list of moving-object candidates with the evidence behind each one.

Anyone can also type coordinates or a name and get a flipbook of every visit SPHEREx has made to that spot, including the five test targets named in the challenge. With it comes the spectrum of whatever sits there, measured on the fly from the same exposures.

It matters because the method is measured, not promised: on 242 square degrees the search recovered 172 of 182 known asteroids brighter than magnitude 17.5, and the site publishes how well people and software do, including where they fail. One example: of 93 unexplained dots re-checked in photos taken two minutes apart, 48 were cosmic-ray hits, 27 faint stars, and one is real.
details:
In short

  • 172 of 182 known asteroids (95%) recovered by the search, a median of 2.3 arcseconds from where the catalogue puts them.
  • A ten-second flipbook of two real NASA SPHEREx photos and one question: did something move? Known asteroids and planted test dots measure every volunteer, and reliable answers weigh more.
  • All five targets named in the challenge are built in, each with a flipbook, a spectrum and its brightness over time.
  • Live at https://dchr.koinotinav.com/skyblink/ and open source at https://github.com/BillSharifzade/sphereX.

What it does

  • Hunt. A feed of two-frame flipbooks. Yes, No, or "I can't tell". The first six are practice with known answers and instant feedback. After that, most patches have no known answer. After a yes you can tap where it moved. The page shows your own record on test patches and what it does to the weight of your answers.
  • Candidates. Patches the search could not explain, ranked by the crowd's estimate that something real moved. Each was checked against the catalogue of known asteroids and comets first. The list downloads as CSV, and its measured dots as Minor Planet Center records for observations from a spacecraft (nothing has been reported there).
  • Explore. Right ascension and declination (degrees or sexagesimal) or an object name. The server reads the frames from NASA's archive and builds the flipbook, with a spectrum and the catalogue layers, in about 20 to 40 seconds. The field of view can be 13 or 26 arcminutes. Coordinates can also be given in the URL, and an /embed/ address gives the bare flipbook for an iframe on any other site.
  • Field view. One patch across time: a flipbook per detector across visits at matched wavelength, a flipbook inside one visit, and stacked flipbooks that add every exposure of a visit to reach fainter. Any set can be blinked, subtracted (Difference) or added (Sum) in the browser. Layers show the Gaia DR3 stars, with an arrow on every fast one, and the WISE sources. Every frame lists its date, detector, wavelength, how much of it is masked and why, and a link to the original NASA file.
  • Spectra. Each SPHEREx exposure sees a spot in one colour. The site measures the object at the centre of a field in up to about 250 exposures and draws the result: the water and methane bands of the brown dwarfs Epsilon Indi B, the methane ice of Pluto. Where SPHEREx came back, the same points show brightness over time at matched colours. The numbers download as CSV.
  • Farther than Pluto. Haumea, Makemake and Eris through one SPHEREx visit each. Eris, 96 times the Earth's distance from the Sun, is too faint for any single photo; added along the path its orbit predicts, it appears.
  • Results. Every measurement with its sample size and its 95% range. A rate is not quoted from fewer than ten answers.

How it works

  1. Reading SPHEREx efficiently. A SPHEREx image file is 65 MB. Our pipeline parses the FITS layout and asks the public cloud mirror only for the bytes it needs, about 2.5 MB per stamp.
  2. Matching colour. Every SPHEREx pixel sees a different wavelength, so the same star looks different from one exposure to the next. The pipeline uses the archive's footprint metadata to choose exposures that put the sky on nearly the same detector rows. Frames in a hunt flipbook differ by about 2%.
  3. Searching. On each pair of full frames it runs a matched filter on native pixels and lists sources that have good data and nothing at the same sky position in the other frame. It excludes flagged pixels, noisy airglow rows, satellite trails, single-pixel hits and the surroundings of bright stars.
  4. Labelling. It asks SkyBoT where every known asteroid and comet is at that moment. Detected known bodies become test tasks with known answers. Unexplained sources become the tasks nobody knows the answer to. Empty patches become controls, and some get a planted mover of known brightness.
  5. Looking again. SPHEREx takes its exposures in bursts, two minutes apart. For every unexplained dot the pipeline reads small windows of the other exposures of the burst. A real object is still there; a cosmic-ray hit is not. Volunteers see this only after they have answered, so it is a second, independent opinion.
  6. Weighing answers. Each volunteer has a hit rate and a false-alarm rate measured on the test tasks. Each unknown patch starts at a 5% chance and every answer updates it with Bayes' rule (the Space Warps method). Three calibrated volunteers at 95% make a candidate.

What we measured

  • 20 pairs of full frames, 242 square degrees near the ecliptic, 1,028,910 sources.
  • 172 of 182 (95%) catalogued asteroids brighter than V = 17.5 recovered. A random position scores 7.7% by chance.
  • Looking again two minutes later: 74 of 74 dots of known asteroids found again (the control). Of 93 unexplained patches: 48 cosmic-ray hits, 27 faint stars, 17 could not be checked, 1 real in one photo only.
  • Brightness over time: R Draconis, saturated in all 243 exposures and followed through a ring of light, fades to 0.42 of its May 2025 brightness by June 2026; RW Aurigae is 1.59 times brighter below 2.4 µm after a year.
  • Eris (V 18.7, 96 AU): at most 4.6 times the noise in a single frame, 7.6 and 8.8 in stacks of 15 or 16 exposures shifted along its path.

The full list, with sample sizes and crowd results computed live, is on the Results page of the site.

Limits, stated plainly

A Planet-Nine-like body would be three to five magnitudes too faint for a single SPHEREx frame. Skyblink finds what single frames can show (asteroids, comets, fast nearby objects). Adding exposures along a path reaches fainter, as Eris shows, but only because its path is known; a blind search over every possible path is not built. Candidates are leads for professional follow-up, not discoveries.

Tools and languages

Python (astropy, numpy, scipy, Pillow) for the pipeline. Rust (axum, tokio, sqlx with SQLite) for the server. TypeScript with Next.js, React and Tailwind CSS for the site. Docker for deployment.

Code and AI use

Open source, Apache 2.0: https://github.com/BillSharifzade/sphereX. The concept and product decisions are ours. The demo video's motion, layout and music were generated with Claude from our prompts, real screenshots and real SPHEREx frames, and it carries a visible mark. No image on the site is AI-generated: every picture is SPHEREx data or a screenshot of the running site.
